title: Picot edging
subtitle: A row of small pointed loops to trim an edge
excerpt: A neat pointed trim: one firm base row, then a row of small picot loops that stand up along the edge like tiny scallops turned to points. Worked here as a short standalone strip in 4-ply cotton, it is the classic finish for collars, cuffs, and lace edges.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passages on picots used to ornament a crochet edge. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The yarn weight, hook size, and gauge are modernised; the picot structure is Victorian.

crochet.gaugeText: 16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. Gauge is not critical for an edging; tension changes the finished length more than the look of the picots.
crochet.finishedSizeText: About 12 cm long and 2 cm deep as written. Lengthen by adding chains to the foundation in multiples of 2.

chartDefinition.title: Picot edging, two rows
chartDefinition.caption: Row 1 is a firm base of double crochet. Row 2 sets a small picot between each pair of anchor stitches.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small decorative loop made by working a few chains and closing them back on themselves, leaving a little point that trims an edge.
A short, firm crochet stitch with no yarn-over before the hook goes in. Called single crochet in the United States.
Wetting or steaming a finished piece and pinning it to shape while it dries, so the stitches settle even and the picots stand up neatly.

content.text: This trim sets a row of small

points along a firm base row. It is the classic finish for collars, cuffs, and the edges of lace, and it is worked here as a short standalone strip so you can learn the spacing before edging a real piece. The pattern is written in UK terms, where double crochet is the short, firm stitch (single crochet in the United States).
About 12 m makes the strip as written. A smooth mercerised cotton such as Scheepjes Catona keeps the picots crisp. Any 4-ply cotton works.
The usual pairing for 4-ply cotton. Drop to 2.75 mm if your tension runs loose.
For weaving in the two tails at the end.
16 double crochet to 10 cm in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. Gauge is not critical for an edging; tension changes the finished length more than it changes the look of the picots.
dc = double crochet (UK), called single crochet in the US
Read the chart alongside the written rows. The chart shows where each picot sits; the written rows give the counts.
Make a foundation chain of 20 chains.
in the 2nd chain from the hook, then 1 dc in each of the next 18 chains. (19 sts)

Ch 1 and turn. Work 1 dc in the first dc. [Ch 3, slip stitch into the 3rd chain from the hook to make a picot, skip 1 dc, 1 dc in the next dc] 9 times. This sets 9 picots between 10 anchor stitches. (10 sts)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail. The strip is complete.
Weave both tails into the back of the base row with the tapestry needle, doubling back once to lock them, then trim. Pin the strip straight and
it so the picots stand up evenly, then leave it to dry.

To edge a real piece, work the first row of double crochet straight into the edge of the item, keeping the count even so the picots space regularly. A larger picot of four or five chains gives a bolder point; spacing a picot every third stitch instead of every second makes a softer, more open trim.
